newsitem.title: USA: Study of Israeli settlements "not public" - U.S..
newsitem.headline: Study of Israeli settlements "not public" - U.S..

text.p: The United States said on Tuesday it had recently studied Israeli settlement activity but declined to confirm a published report that the study had found more than a quarter of settler homes were empty.
"I can't speak specifically about this report, because it has not been made public," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters.
"But we have from time to time and just recently tried to establish a basis of information for ourselves and for the Congress on this issue, and we've done that," he said.

Israel's Haaretz daily said Washington, citing U.S. data showing that a large number of homes were lying vacant, believed it was not necessary to expand Jewish settlements. That report has caused controversy in Israel, where Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu dismissed it as groundless.

The settlement issue has taken centre stage in a crisis over the Israeli-Palestinian talks, deadlocked since Netanyahu broke ground in March for a new Jewish enclave in East Jerusalem, which Israel captured in 1967.
The Palestinians said last week the United States had abandoned its long-held opposition to settlements as "obstacles to peace."

At a news briefing, Burns confirmed that legislation under which the United States provided Israel with housing loan guarantees imposed a responsibility on Washington to monitor settlement activity, including such factors as construction and occupancy. But "I can't speak about this (newspaper) report," he said.
Burns said he did not believe the issue came up in U.S. peace envoy Dennis Ross' talks in the Middle East last week.
Later, a senior U.S. official, who asked not to be identified, said, "I'm not sure about the full accuracy of this particular report in the Israeli press."
Ross' nine-day mediation mission failed to move the talks forward, with each side blaming the other for the deadlock.

Israel Radio suggested the leak of the study appeared timed to coincide with Israel's refusal, in meetings with Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and Ross, to bow to U.S. pressure to curb Jewish settlement construction.

Haaretz said the U.S. study, compiled partly from data obtained from observation satellites, showed that 26 percent of apartments in the West Bank, 56 percent of those in Gaza and 28 percent of those on the Golan Heights were vacant.
The West Bank is home to some 130,000 Jews, living in settlements among 2 million Palestinians in the territories Israel captured in the 1967 Middle East war.
Haaretz said U.S. officials were concerned that there were at least 11,000 homes in stages of approval, apart from the 6,500 homes due to be built at the disputed East Jerusalem site.
